column9: stem
column28: explanation
column29: hint

column9: Why do biologists use taxonomy?
column14: To organize millions of kinds of organisms so they can be named, identified and compared
column15: To count how many individuals live in a forest
column16: To rank organisms by how valuable they are to people, so the most useful ones can be protected
column17: To change the traits of organisms
column28: There are millions of kinds of organisms. Taxonomy sorts and names them so scientists can identify them and compare them. It does not rank organisms by value or count populations; counting individuals is ecology.
column29: Think about how a library sorts books so you can find the one you want.

column9: What does it mean to classify things?
column14: To give each one a number
column15: To measure how big each one is
column16: To organize or group them based on similarities
column17: To study how they change over time and record the changes
column28: Classifying means organizing or grouping things based on how they are alike. Measuring or numbering things does not put them into groups.
column29: Think of how a grocery store puts the cereals in one aisle and the fruit in another.

column9: In a scientific name, the first word is the ___ name.
column28: The first word of a scientific name is the genus, and it is always capitalized. The second word is the species name. Mixing up the order is the common mistake.
column29: The first word names a group of similar species.

column9: The scientific name of the red maple is *Acer rubrum*. Which word is the genus?
column28: The genus is the first word of a scientific name and is capitalized: *Acer*. The second word, *rubrum*, is the species name. Red and maple are parts of the common name, not the scientific name.
column29: Which word comes first and starts with a capital letter?

column9: The system that gives every species a two-word scientific name is called ___ nomenclature.
column28: Binomial nomenclature means "two-name naming": every species gets a genus name and a species name. "Dichotomous" also has to do with two, but it describes a key with two choices at each step, not a naming system.
column29: "Bi" means two and "nomen" means name.

column9: In the 1700s, a Swedish scientist gave the gray wolf the two-part name *Canis lupus* using his new naming system. Who was he?
column28: Carl Linnaeus set up the classification and two-name naming system that biologists still use. Darwin is known for natural selection, Hooke for naming cells and Pasteur for work on germs.
column29: He is the father of taxonomy and lived in Sweden.

column9: Linnaeus lived long before anyone knew about DNA. What did he use to sort organisms into groups?
column14: Only the places where they lived, such as forests or lakes
column15: Physical and structural similarities and differences
column16: Their common names in different languages
column28: Linnaeus grouped organisms by their physical and structural traits: what their bodies look like and how they are built. DNA had not been discovered yet, so choosing DNA is the common mistake. Habitat and common names are not reliable ways to classify.
column29: He could only use what he could see and measure.

column9: Why are scientific names written in Latin?
column14: Latin was the only language Linnaeus could write
column15: Latin words are always shorter than English words, so names are easier to write
column16: Only Latin has words for plants and animals
column17: Latin is no longer spoken in daily life, so its words don't change
column28: Living languages change over time, but Latin is no longer spoken in daily life, so a Latin name stays the same. Latin names are not always shorter; many are long.
column29: Think about what happens to the words of a language that people still use every day.

column9: Which shows the correct way to print the scientific name of the white-tailed deer?
column28: The genus (*Odocoileus*) comes first with a capital letter, and the species name (*virginianus*) comes second in all lowercase. Capitalizing the species name is the most common mistake.
column29: Only one word gets a capital letter. Which one comes first?

column9: A field guide lists a bird down to the most specific level of classification, so only one kind of bird fits. Which level is that?
column28: Species is the most specific level: it holds just one kind of organism. Kingdom is the broadest level. Genus is close, but a genus can hold several similar species.
column29: It is the last level in the list, and it is the second word of a scientific name.

column9: In the levels of classification, the level just below kingdom and just above class is ___.
column28: The order is kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. Phylum sits between kingdom and class. Putting class before phylum is a common slip.
column29: In the memory trick "King Philip Came Over For Good Soup," which word comes second?

column9: Lions (*Panthera leo*) and tigers (*Panthera tigris*) belong to the same genus. Type the name of that genus: ___
column28: The genus is the first word of each name, and both names begin with *Panthera*. *Leo* and *tigris* are the species names.
column29: Look for the word the two names have in common.

column9: A student remembers the levels with the sentence "Kings Play Chess On Fine Grain Sand." What level does the O stand for?
column28: Kings Play Chess On Fine Grain Sand stands for Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species. O is order. Organism and organ start with O but are not classification levels.
column29: Each word starts with the same letter as one level, in the same order. O is the fourth word.

column9: How many kingdoms are in the classification system used in Biology class?
column28: There are six kingdoms: Animalia, Plantae, Fungi, Protista, Eubacteria and Archaebacteria. Answering 3 confuses kingdoms with the three domains, and older books used 5 kingdoms.
column29: Two of the kingdoms are kinds of bacteria. Count those plus plants, animals, fungi and protists.

column9: Counting from kingdom down to species, how many levels of classification are there?
column28: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species makes 7 levels. Counting the six kingdoms instead of the levels (6) is a common mix-up.
column29: Count the words in "King Philip Came Over For Good Soup."

column9: Which kingdom contains mushrooms, molds and yeasts?
column28: Mushrooms, molds and yeasts are all fungi. Mushrooms grow from the ground and cannot move, so students often call them plants, but they do not make their own food by photosynthesis.
column29: These organisms absorb food from what they grow on instead of making it.

column9: Which kingdom contains organisms that are multicellular, make their own food by photosynthesis and have cell walls made of cellulose?
column28: Plants are multicellular autotrophs with cellulose cell walls. Fungi have cell walls but do not photosynthesize, animals have no cell walls, and bacteria are single-celled prokaryotes.
column29: Which kingdom contains trees and grass?

column9: A single-celled prokaryote lives in a boiling hot spring that has no oxygen. Its genetics are more complex than ordinary bacteria. Which kingdom does it most likely belong to?
column28: Most archaebacteria live in extreme environments, most do not need oxygen, and they have more complex genetics than eubacteria. Eubacteria are also prokaryotes, so that is the common wrong answer, but they mostly live in ordinary places. Protists and fungi are eukaryotes.
column29: "Archae" means ancient. Which kingdom is known for extreme places?

column9: Which kingdom includes organisms that are multicellular, eat other organisms for food, have no cell walls and usually can move from place to place?
column28: Animals are multicellular heterotrophs with no cell walls, and most can move. Fungi are heterotrophs too, but they have cell walls and cannot move.
column29: Which kingdom are you in?

column9: *Escherichia coli* (E. coli) is a common prokaryote with a strong cell wall that lives in human intestines. Which kingdom is it in?
column28: E. coli is a prokaryote that lives in an ordinary place (your gut) and has a strong cell wall, so it is a eubacterium. Archaebacteria are also prokaryotes, which makes them the tempting wrong answer, but most of them live in extreme environments.
column29: Both bacteria kingdoms are prokaryotes. Which one lives in ordinary places?

column9: *Amoeba proteus* is a single-celled organism from pond water. Its cell has a nucleus, but it has no tissues or organ systems. Which kingdom is it in?
column28: An amoeba is a single-celled eukaryote, which puts it in Protista. It moves and eats like an animal, which makes Animalia tempting, but animals are multicellular. It has a nucleus, so it is not a bacterium.
column29: It has a nucleus, so rule out bacteria. Then ask: one cell or many?

column9: A hiker finds a beetle she has never seen before and uses a dichotomous key. What will the key help her do?
column15: Find out how old the beetle is
column16: Identify the beetle by making a series of two-choice decisions
column17: Decide which kingdom the beetle should be moved to, based on its size and color
column28: A dichotomous key is an identification tool. At each step you pick one of two choices until the key gives you the organism's name. It does not measure, age or reclassify anything.
column29: "Key" here means a tool that unlocks an organism's name.

column9: The word "dichotomous" means divided into ___ parts.
column28: Dichotomous means divided into two parts, which is why every step of a dichotomous key has two choices. Some students guess three or more because a key has many steps, but each step has only two choices.
column29: How many choices are there at each step of the key?

column9: Each named group at any level of classification, such as the class Mammalia or the genus *Canis*, is called a ___.
column28: A taxon (plural: taxa) is any named group in classification, at any level. "Taxonomy" is the science of naming and classifying, not the name of one group.
column29: It is the root of the word taxonomy.

column9: Which pair of organisms is in the same genus?
column14: *Acer rubrum* (red maple) and *Quercus rubra* (northern red oak)
column28: Organisms in the same genus share the first word of their scientific names: both bears are *Ursus*. The maple and oak have similar second words (*rubrum*, *rubra*), but the second word is the species name, not the genus.
column29: Compare the FIRST word of each name.

column9: Two organisms belong to the same genus. Which other level must they also share?
column28: Each level fits inside the one above it, so two organisms in the same genus are also in the same family, order, class, phylum and kingdom. They do not have to share a species; that level is below genus.
column29: Genus fits inside a bigger group. Which level is right above genus?

column9: If two organisms are in the same order, they must also be in the same class.
column28: True. Every order fits inside one class, so organisms in the same order share their class, phylum and kingdom too. The reverse is not true: organisms in the same class can be in different orders.
column29: Is order above or below class? Smaller groups fit inside bigger ones.

column9: What does the second word of a scientific name (the species name) usually describe?
column14: The number of species in its genus
column15: The year the organism was discovered
column16: The kingdom the organism belongs to, such as Plantae for plants or Animalia for animals
column17: A characteristic of the organism, such as its color or where it lives
column28: The species name usually describes a trait. For example, *rubrum* in *Acer rubrum* means red. The genus, not the species name, tells you the group of similar species, and neither word names the kingdom.
column29: In *Acer rubrum* (red maple), *rubrum* means red.

column9: An earthworm and a bald eagle are both in Kingdom Animalia. What does this tell you?
column14: They are in the same genus, because kingdom is the most specific level
column16: They share the broadest level, but they can still be very different
column28: Kingdom is the broadest level, so organisms in the same kingdom can be very different. Assuming that sharing a kingdom makes two organisms close relatives is the common mistake. Close relatives share many levels, down to family or genus.
column29: Kingdom holds the most kinds of organisms. Is that a big group or a small one?

column9: The same bird is called the "house sparrow" in English, "gorrión" in Spanish and "Haussperling" in German. Scientists everywhere call it *Passer domesticus*. What does this example show?
column14: Spanish is the official language of science, so the Spanish name is correct
column15: Birds do not have scientific names
column16: A scientific name is the same in every language, so it avoids confusion
column17: Common names are more exact than scientific names, because everyone already knows them
column28: One organism can have many common names, but it has only one scientific name, used in every language. That is why scientists use scientific names. Scientific names are Latin, not Spanish.
column29: Which name would a scientist in any country recognize?

column9: A seahorse is a fish, but a silverfish is an insect. What does this show about common names?
column14: Seahorses and silverfish are in the same class
column15: Insects and fish are classified together in the same class, because both can be called fish
column16: Common names can mislead; "fish" in a name doesn't tell you what group an organism is in
column17: Common names always match an organism's kingdom
column28: Common names often mislead: a silverfish is an insect, and a seahorse is a fish even though it is named after a horse. Trusting the common name is the mistake; the scientific classification shows the real group.
column29: Is a silverfish really a fish?

column9: Which kingdoms are made of prokaryotes? Select all that apply.
column28: Only the two bacteria kingdoms, Eubacteria and Archaebacteria, are prokaryotes (cells with no nucleus). Protists are often tiny and single-celled, so students pick Protista, but protist cells have a nucleus.
column29: Prokaryotes have no nucleus. Which kingdoms are bacteria?

column9: Put these levels in order from the most specific to the broadest.
column28: From most specific to broadest: species, genus, family, order, class. This is the usual list read backward. Swapping order and family is a common slip.
column29: Start with the second word of a scientific name, then move up one level at a time.

column9: The striped skunk is *Mephitis mephitis*. A student writes it as *Mephitis Mephitis*. What did the student do wrong?
column28: The species name is always lowercase, so it should be *Mephitis mephitis*. Repeating the same word is allowed (the bison is *Bison bison*), so that is not the error.
column29: Which word of a scientific name is always lowercase?

column9: Which is the definition of taxonomy?
column14: The branch of biology that classifies and names living things
column15: The preserving and mounting of dead animals
column16: The study of how traits pass from parents to offspring
column17: The study of how organisms interact with each other and their environment
column28: Taxonomy is the branch of biology that classifies and names organisms. The other choices describe ecology, taxidermy and genetics. Taxidermy sounds like taxonomy, which makes it the common mix-up.
column29: "Taxo" means arrangement and "-nomy" means naming.

column9: Which level is directly above species?
column28: The last two levels are genus, then species, and they are the two words of a scientific name. Family comes before genus.
column29: A scientific name is made of the last two levels.

column9: The potato is *Solanum tuberosum* and the tomato is *Solanum lycopersicum*. Which statement is true?
column14: They share only their kingdom, because their species names differ
column16: They are in the same genus, so they are also in the same family
column28: Both names start with *Solanum*, so they share a genus, and every level above it. Their species names differ, so they are different species. Sharing only a kingdom would mean their genus names were different too.
column29: Compare the first word, then think about which levels sit above genus.

column9: Which list names the three domains?
column28: The three domains are Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya, and they sit above the kingdoms. Plantae, Animalia and Fungi are kingdoms, and Kingdom, Phylum and Class are levels.
column29: Domains are the biggest groups of all. Two are kinds of prokaryotes.

column9: Domain Eukarya contains every organism whose cells have a nucleus. Which kingdom is NOT in Domain Eukarya?
column28: Eubacteria are prokaryotes (no nucleus), so they belong to Domain Bacteria. Fungi, protists and plants all have a nucleus. Protista is the common wrong pick because many protists are tiny, but their cells still have a nucleus.
column29: Which choice has no nucleus?

column9: A field guide lists the black-capped chickadee as *Poecile atricapillus*. How should a student write the name by hand in her notes?
column14: POECILE ATRICAPILLUS, in all capital letters
column15: Poecile Atricapillus, with the name underlined
column17: Poecile atricapillus, with the name underlined
column28: A scientific name is italicized in print and underlined when written by hand, with only the genus capitalized. Capitalizing both words is the common mistake, even when the underline is right.
column29: You can't write in italics by hand. What do you do instead?

column9: As you move from kingdom down to species, what happens to the groups?
column14: The organisms in each group become less alike as the groups get smaller
column15: Each group holds fewer kinds of organisms, and they are more alike
column16: Every group holds the same number of organisms, no matter which level it is
column17: Each group holds more kinds of organisms
column28: The levels narrow down like an address: kingdom is huge and varied, and species is one kind of organism. Thinking that the lower levels hold more organisms is the common mistake.
column29: Compare Kingdom Animalia with the genus *Canis*. Which holds more kinds of animals?

column9: Organisms are sorted into kingdoms partly by how they get food. What is an organism that makes its own food called?
column28: An autotroph makes its own food, usually by photosynthesis. A heterotroph has to take in food, and a decomposer is a heterotroph that breaks down dead material. Prokaryote describes cell type, not how food is gotten.
column29: "Auto" means self, as in a car you drive yourself.

column9: Which pair of organisms is in the same kingdom?
column28: Ferns and mosses are both multicellular plants that photosynthesize, so both are in Plantae. Mushrooms are fungi, amoebas are protists and E. coli is a eubacterium.
column29: Put each organism in its kingdom first, then look for a match.

column9: Two organisms in the same class are always in the same genus.
column28: False. Class is a broad level, and it holds many genera. A cat and a mouse are both in class Mammalia but are in different genera. The rule only works the other way: same genus means same class.
column29: Is class a big group or a small group?

column9: Match each part of a scientific name to the rule for writing it.
column14: Genus :: The first word, always capitalized
column15: Species name :: The second word, always lowercase
column16: The whole name in print :: Written in italics
column28: The genus comes first with a capital letter, the species name comes second in lowercase, and the whole name is italicized in print. Capitalizing the species name is the most common mistake.
column29: Think of *Homo sapiens*: which word has the capital letter?

column9: Match each kingdom to its description.
column14: Archaebacteria :: Prokaryotes; most live in extreme environments
column15: Eubacteria :: Prokaryotes with strong cell walls; most are harmless and many are helpful
column16: Protista :: Eukaryotes without complex organ systems; one cell or many
column17: Fungi :: Non-moving heterotrophs that absorb nutrients from organic material
column18: Plantae :: Multicellular autotrophs with cell walls made of cellulose
column19: Animalia :: Multicellular heterotrophs with no cell walls
column28: Start with the two prokaryote kingdoms (extreme places for Archaebacteria, ordinary places for Eubacteria). Then sort the eukaryotes: protists are simple, fungi absorb food, plants make food and animals eat food and lack cell walls. Swapping fungi and plants is the most common mistake.
column29: Sort by cell type first (prokaryote or eukaryote), then by how each kingdom gets food.

column9: Match each domain to the kingdom or kingdoms it contains.
column16: Eukarya :: Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia
column28: Domain Bacteria holds Kingdom Eubacteria, Domain Archaea holds Kingdom Archaebacteria, and Domain Eukarya holds the four kingdoms whose cells have a nucleus. Matching Bacteria with Archaebacteria because of the word "bacteria" is the common mistake.
column29: Look at the beginning of each word: Archaea and Archae-bacteria.

column9: Match each organism to its kingdom.
column16: Paramecium (*Paramecium caudatum*), a single-celled eukaryote :: Protista
column18: The bacteria that cause strep throat :: Eubacteria
column19: A methane-making prokaryote from oxygen-free swamp mud :: Archaebacteria
column28: Yeast is a fungus even though it is single-celled, the maple is a plant, the paramecium is a protist, the monarch is an animal, strep bacteria are eubacteria, and methane makers from oxygen-free mud are archaebacteria. Calling yeast a protist because it has one cell is the common mistake.
column29: Do the familiar ones (maple, butterfly) first, then use cell type for the tiny ones.

column9: Which kingdoms contain ONLY multicellular organisms? Select all that apply.
column28: Every plant and every animal is multicellular. Fungi is the common wrong pick: mushrooms are multicellular, but yeasts are single-celled fungi. Protista has both single-celled and multicellular members, and bacteria are single-celled.
column29: Think of yeast before you choose Fungi.

column9: Which of these species names are written correctly in print? Select all that apply.
column28: A correct species name has two words, the genus capitalized and the species name lowercase. *Bison bison* is correct even though the word repeats. *Quercus Alba* capitalizes the species name, *acer saccharum* does not capitalize the genus, and *Canis* is only a genus, not a full species name.
column29: Check three things: two words, capital first word, lowercase second word.

column9: Why do scientists use scientific names instead of common names? Select all that apply.
column14: Each species has only one scientific name
column15: A scientific name is the same in every language
column16: A scientific name tells you exactly where the organism lives
column17: Scientific names are always shorter than common names
column18: Latin does not change over time
column28: Scientific names are the same in every language, each species has just one, and Latin is not changing. A scientific name does not give an exact location, and many scientific names are longer than common names.
column29: Think about a scientist in Mexico and a scientist in Germany talking about the same bird.

column9: The bobcat is *Lynx rufus* and the Canada lynx is *Lynx canadensis*. Which levels must they share? Select all that apply.
column28: They share the genus *Lynx*, so they also share every level above it: family, order, class, phylum and kingdom. Their species names (*rufus* and *canadensis*) differ, so they are different species.
column29: Find the level they share in their names, then include every level above it.

column9: Four cats: lion (*Panthera leo*), leopard (*Panthera pardus*), bobcat (*Lynx rufus*) and house cat (*Felis catus*). All four are in family Felidae. Which two are most closely related?
column28: The lion and leopard share the genus *Panthera*, the most specific level any pair here shares. Every other pair shares only the family. Picking the bobcat and house cat because they are similar in size is the common mistake.
column29: All four share the family. Which pair shares a level below family?

column9: The eastern chipmunk and the gray squirrel are both in family Sciuridae. The beaver is in the same order (Rodentia) but a different family. Which pair is more closely related?
column15: All three are equally related as rodents
column16: The gray squirrel and the beaver
column17: The chipmunk and the gray squirrel
column28: The chipmunk and squirrel share a family, which is more specific than the order all three share. Thinking that all three are equally related because they are all rodents is the common mistake.
column29: Family is below order. Which pair shares the smaller group?

column9: The gray wolf (*Canis lupus*) and the coyote (*Canis latrans*) are in the same genus. Of the seven levels from kingdom to species, how many do they share?
column28: Sharing the genus means they also share family, order, class, phylum and kingdom: 6 levels. Only the species is different. Answering 7 would mean they were the same species; answering 2 counts only the two words of the name.
column29: Count kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus. Which level is different?

column9:
Tree key:
1a. Leaves are needles → go to 2
1b. Leaves are broad and flat → go to 3
2a. Needles grow in bundles of 5 → eastern white pine (*Pinus strobus*)
2b. Needles grow in bundles of 2 → red pine (*Pinus resinosa*)
3a. Leaves grow in pairs across from each other on the twig → sugar maple (*Acer saccharum*)
3b. Leaves grow one at a time, alternating along the twig → red oak (*Quercus rubra*)
A tree has broad, flat leaves that grow one at a time, alternating along the twig. What is it?
column28: Broad, flat leaves → 1b → step 3. Leaves alternating one at a time → 3b → red oak. Picking the sugar maple means 3a and 3b were mixed up: maple leaves grow in opposite pairs.
column29: Start at 1. Read both choices before you pick one.

column9:
Tree key:
1a. Leaves are needles → go to 2
1b. Leaves are broad and flat → go to 3
2a. Needles grow in bundles of 5 → eastern white pine (*Pinus strobus*)
2b. Needles grow in bundles of 2 → red pine (*Pinus resinosa*)
3a. Leaves grow in pairs across from each other on the twig → sugar maple (*Acer saccharum*)
3b. Leaves grow one at a time, alternating along the twig → red oak (*Quercus rubra*)
Which path through the key leads to the eastern white pine?
column28: Needles → 1a → step 2. Bundles of 5 → 2a → eastern white pine. Choosing 1a → 2b ends at the red pine, which has needles in bundles of 2.
column29: Pines have needles. Which step deals with needles?

column9: A student says, "Cats and dogs are both in order Carnivora, so they must be in the same genus." What is wrong with this reasoning?
column14: Nothing is wrong; they are in the same genus because they share an order
column15: Cats and dogs are in different kingdoms, so they can't share any level
column16: Order is a narrower level than genus
column17: Sharing a broad level does not mean sharing a narrower one
column28: Genus is inside order, not the other way around. Organisms in the same order can be in different families and genera: cats are *Felis* and dogs are *Canis*. Thinking that order is narrower than genus is the root of the mistake.
column29: Is order above or below genus? Can a big group hold several smaller groups?

column9: Two organisms share the same class but are in different orders. Which must be true?
column14: They also share a phylum and a kingdom
column16: They share no other levels besides their class
column28: Class sits inside phylum, which sits inside kingdom, so they share those too. Since their orders differ, they cannot share family or genus, which are below order.
column29: Which levels are above class, and which are below order?

column9: Put the steps for using a dichotomous key in order.
column14: Go to the step that your choice points to
column15: Keep going until the key gives you the organism's name
column16: Pick the choice that describes your organism
column28: You start at step 1, read BOTH choices, pick the one that fits, follow it to the next step, and repeat until you reach a name. Picking the first choice that sounds right without reading the second one is a common mistake.
column29: You can't follow a choice until you've picked one.

column9: Put the classification of the bobcat in order from broadest to most specific.
column28: Kingdom, class, order, family, genus, species: Animalia, Mammalia, Carnivora, Felidae, *Lynx*, *Lynx rufus*. (Phylum Chordata would go between kingdom and class.) Putting family before order is a common slip.
column29: Use the level names in parentheses and King Philip Came Over For Good Soup.

column9: Which pair of organisms shares the FEWEST classification levels?
column14: A sugar maple and a monarch butterfly
column15: A lion and a house cat
column17: A gray wolf and a coyote
column28: A maple is a plant and a monarch is an animal, so they are in different kingdoms and share none of the seven levels. The other pairs are in the same family or genus.
column29: Which pair is not even in the same kingdom?

column9: Which group contains the MOST different kinds of organisms?
column28: Class is the broadest of these levels, so it holds the most kinds of organisms: every mammal. Carnivora, Canidae and *Canis* are smaller groups inside it. Picking genus because it "has the most specific name" mixes up specific and broad.
column29: Name the level of each group, then pick the broadest level.

column9: Order Primates includes humans, chimpanzees and lemurs. Family Hominidae includes humans, chimpanzees and gorillas, but not lemurs. Why?
column15: A family is broader than an order, so it holds more kinds of organisms
column17: A family is a smaller, more specific group inside an order
column28: Each order is split into families, so a family holds only some of the order's members. Lemurs are primates, just in a different family. Thinking family is broader than order is the common mistake.
column29: Is family above or below order?

column9: A pond organism is a single eukaryotic cell that makes its own food with chloroplasts. It has no roots, stems or leaves. Which kingdom is it in?
column28: It has a nucleus and is single-celled, so it is a protist (like Euglena). Making food by photosynthesis tempts students to pick Plantae, but every plant is multicellular. Bacteria have no nucleus, and fungi do not make their own food.
column29: Plants and this organism both photosynthesize. How many cells do plants have?

column9: Bread mold grows on an old slice of bread. It cannot move, does not photosynthesize and absorbs nutrients from the bread. Which kingdom is it in?
column28: Absorbing nutrients from organic material without moving is the mark of Fungi. Molds grow and stay in place like plants, but they do not photosynthesize, so Plantae is the common wrong answer.
column29: How does it get its food?

column9: Yeast is single-celled and a mushroom is multicellular, yet both are in Kingdom Fungi. What do they share that puts them together?
column14: Both are eukaryotes that cannot move and absorb nutrients from organic material
column17: Both make their own food by photosynthesis, the way plants do, and store it as starch
column28: Kingdom Fungi is defined by how its members get food (absorbing it) and by being non-moving eukaryotes, not by cell number. Fungi do not photosynthesize, are not prokaryotes and do have cell walls.
column29: Number of cells is not the deciding trait here. What about how they eat?

column9: Brook trout (*Salvelinus fontinalis*) and lake trout (*Salvelinus namaycush*) share a genus, but rainbow trout are *Oncorhynchus mykiss*. Of the three, the least closely related to the other two is the ___ trout.
column28: The brook and lake trout share the genus *Salvelinus*, but the rainbow trout is in a different genus, *Oncorhynchus*. All three are called trout, but the common name does not show how closely related they are.
column29: Compare the first word of each scientific name.

column9: A group of closely related genera (the plural of genus) makes up a ___.
column28: Genera are grouped into a family, the level just above genus. Answering "species" goes the wrong direction: species is below genus.
column29: In King Philip Came Over For Good Soup, step one word back from Good.

column9: How many of the six kingdoms belong to Domain Eukarya?
column28: Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia all have cells with a nucleus, so 4 kingdoms are in Eukarya. The other two (Eubacteria and Archaebacteria) are in their own domains. Answering 3 often leaves out Protista.
column29: Count the kingdoms whose cells have a nucleus.

column9: One student says a killer whale should be classified with fish because it swims and has fins. A second student says it is a mammal because it breathes with lungs, gives birth to live young and feeds them milk. Whose reasoning matches how taxonomists classify?
column14: Neither, because whales are not classified
column15: Both, because whales belong to two classes
column16: The second student, because classification uses many shared body traits, not just habitat or swimming
column17: The first student, because fins and swimming are the traits that matter most for animals that live in water
column28: Taxonomists compare many structural traits. Lungs, live birth and milk are traits shared with mammals, so killer whales are mammals. Grouping by where an animal lives or one trait like fins is the common mistake.
column29: Which student used more traits about how the body is built?

column9: Scientists find a new kind of bumblebee and place it in the genus *Bombus*. What can they predict right away?
column14: It is the same species as every other *Bombus* bee
column15: It will get the same species name as the other bumblebees, since it is in the same genus
column16: It shares many traits with other *Bombus* bees and every level above genus with them
column17: It could be in any kingdom
column28: Placing an organism in a genus tells you it is similar to the other species there and shares every level above genus. A new species gets its own species name, so it cannot share one with the other bees.
column29: Each species in a genus has its own second name.

column9: Which traits do biologists use to sort organisms into the six kingdoms? Select all that apply.
column15: Whether its cells have a nucleus
column17: Whether it is single-celled or multicellular
column18: Whether it makes its own food or takes in food
column28: Kingdoms are sorted by cell type (prokaryote or eukaryote), number of cells, and how organisms get food. Color and size vary a lot even within one species, so they are not used to place organisms in kingdoms.
column29: Which traits are about cells and food?

column9: Why is "1a. The organism is pretty / 1b. The organism is ugly" a poor step for a dichotomous key?
column14: It has only two choices, but a good key step needs at least three to pick from
column15: The choices are opinions, so different people would pick differently
column28: Every step of a good key uses traits anyone can observe the same way, such as "has wings" or "has no wings." Pretty and ugly are opinions. Having only two choices is not a flaw; that is what dichotomous means.
column29: Would you and a friend always choose the same answer?

column9: Modern taxonomists can compare DNA, which Linnaeus could not. When DNA shows two organisms are more closely related than their body shapes suggested, what do taxonomists do?
column15: Reclassify them so the groups better match how they are related
column16: Ignore the DNA and keep the old groups, because Linnaeus already decided them
column28: Classification changes when new evidence appears. DNA is strong evidence of how related organisms are, so taxonomists move organisms into groups that fit it. Thinking classification is fixed forever is the common mistake.
column29: Is science allowed to change its mind when it finds new evidence?

column9:
A classification table lists four mammals:
A: order Carnivora, family Canidae, genus *Vulpes*
B: order Carnivora, family Felidae, genus *Lynx*
C: order Carnivora, family Canidae, genus *Canis*
D: order Rodentia, family Sciuridae, genus *Sciurus*
Which organism is most closely related to C?
column14: B and D are equally close
column28: A and C share the family Canidae, which is more specific than the order that B shares with C. D is in a different order, so it is the most distant. Choosing "B and D are equally close" ignores that B at least shares the order.
column29: Go down the levels and see how far C matches each organism.

column9:
Humans: Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Primates, Hominidae, *Homo*, *sapiens*.
Chimpanzees: Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Primates, Hominidae, *Pan*, *troglodytes*.
How many of the seven levels do humans and chimpanzees share?
column28: They match from kingdom through family (Animalia, Chordata, Mammalia, Primates, Hominidae): 5 levels. They split at genus. Answering 6 counts genus by mistake.
column29: Go down both lists together and stop at the first level that is different.

column9: Organisms X and Y share a kingdom, phylum and class, but they are in different orders. How many of the seven levels do they NOT share?
column28: They share 3 levels (kingdom, phylum, class). Once the orders differ, everything below is different too: order, family, genus and species, so 7 − 3 = 4. Answering 1 counts only the order.
column29: If the orders are different, can the families be the same?

column9: A dichotomous key identifies 9 different organisms. Every step has exactly two choices, and each organism is at the end of exactly one path. How many numbered steps does the key have?
column28: Each step splits one group into two, adding one more group. Going from 1 group (all 9 organisms) to 9 single organisms takes 9 − 1 = 8 steps. Answering 9 assumes one step per organism, and answering 4 or 5 counts how many steps one path needs.
column29: Try a smaller key: how many steps does a key for 2 organisms need? For 3?

column9:
Kingdom key:
1a. Cells have no nucleus → go to 2
1b. Cells have a nucleus → go to 3
2a. Lives in extreme places, such as boiling springs or very salty water → Archaebacteria
2b. Lives in ordinary places, such as soil or the human body → Eubacteria
3a. Makes its own food by photosynthesis → go to 4
3b. Does not make its own food → go to 5
4a. Many-celled, with cellulose cell walls and organized tissues → Plantae
4b. Single-celled, or many-celled without organized tissues → Protista
5a. Has cell walls and absorbs nutrients from what it grows on → Fungi
5b. Has no cell walls → go to 6
6a. Single-celled → Protista
6b. Many-celled, and most can move → Animalia
A pond organism is a single cell with a nucleus. It has no chloroplasts and no cell wall, and it crawls by stretching out its cytoplasm. Where does the key lead?
column28: Nucleus → 1b. No chloroplasts → 3b. No cell wall → 5b. Single-celled → 6a → Protista. Choosing Animalia because the organism moves skips the last step, which asks about the number of cells.
column29: Work every step. Moving is not one of the choices until the very end.

column9:
Kingdom key:
1a. Cells have no nucleus → go to 2
1b. Cells have a nucleus → go to 3
2a. Lives in extreme places, such as boiling springs or very salty water → Archaebacteria
2b. Lives in ordinary places, such as soil or the human body → Eubacteria
3a. Makes its own food by photosynthesis → go to 4
3b. Does not make its own food → go to 5
4a. Many-celled, with cellulose cell walls and organized tissues → Plantae
4b. Single-celled, or many-celled without organized tissues → Protista
5a. Has cell walls and absorbs nutrients from what it grows on → Fungi
5b. Has no cell walls → go to 6
6a. Single-celled → Protista
6b. Many-celled, and most can move → Animalia
A student keys out baker's yeast, a single-celled fungus with a cell wall, and ends at Protista (6a). At which step did the student make the wrong choice?
column28: Yeast goes 1b (nucleus) → 3b (no photosynthesis) → 5a (cell wall, absorbs nutrients) → Fungi. The student must have picked 5b, "has no cell walls," to reach step 6. Blaming step 6 is the common mistake: once at step 6, single-celled was the right choice, but the student should never have gotten there.
column29: Walk yeast through the key yourself and see where your path leaves the student's.

column9:
Kingdom key:
1a. Cells have no nucleus → go to 2
1b. Cells have a nucleus → go to 3
2a. Lives in extreme places, such as boiling springs or very salty water → Archaebacteria
2b. Lives in ordinary places, such as soil or the human body → Eubacteria
3a. Makes its own food by photosynthesis → go to 4
3b. Does not make its own food → go to 5
4a. Many-celled, with cellulose cell walls and organized tissues → Plantae
4b. Single-celled, or many-celled without organized tissues → Protista
5a. Has cell walls and absorbs nutrients from what it grows on → Fungi
5b. Has no cell walls → go to 6
6a. Single-celled → Protista
6b. Many-celled, and most can move → Animalia
Put the choices for keying out an earthworm in the order you would make them.
column15: 3b. Does not make its own food
column28: An earthworm has cells with a nucleus (1b), eats instead of making food (3b), has no cell walls (5b) and is many-celled (6b), so it keys out as Animalia. Jumping straight to 6b because "it moves" skips the steps that lead there.
column29: Begin at step 1 and follow each arrow to the next step number.

column9:
Invertebrate key:
1a. Has jointed legs → go to 2
1b. Has no legs → go to 4
2a. Has 6 legs → go to 3
2b. Has 8 legs → yellow garden spider (*Argiope aurantia*)
3a. Wings are covered with colorful scales → monarch butterfly (*Danaus plexippus*)
3b. Wings are clear, without scales → honeybee (*Apis mellifera*)
4a. Body is made of many ring-shaped segments → earthworm (*Lumbricus terrestris*)
4b. Body is not segmented and carries a shell → garden snail
Which path through the key leads to the honeybee?
column28: Jointed legs → 1a. Six legs → 2a. Clear wings without scales → 3b → honeybee. The path 1a → 2a → 3a ends at the monarch, which also has 6 legs, so stopping one step short or picking the wrong wing type is the common mistake.
column29: Honeybees are insects with 6 legs and see-through wings.

column9:
Invertebrate key:
1a. Has jointed legs → go to 2
1b. Has no legs → go to 4
2a. Has 6 legs → go to 3
2b. Has 8 legs → yellow garden spider (*Argiope aurantia*)
3a. Wings are covered with colorful scales → monarch butterfly (*Danaus plexippus*)
3b. Wings are clear, without scales → honeybee (*Apis mellifera*)
4a. Body is made of many ring-shaped segments → earthworm (*Lumbricus terrestris*)
4b. Body is not segmented and carries a shell → garden snail
A student uses this key on a centipede, which has many more than 8 jointed legs. What happens?
column14: Step 1 sends it to 1b because it is not an insect
column15: At step 2 neither choice fits, because the key was not built to include centipedes
column16: The key identifies it as a yellow garden spider, because it has more than 6 jointed legs
column17: The key identifies it as an earthworm
column28: The centipede has jointed legs, so it goes to step 2, but it has neither 6 nor 8 legs. A key can only identify the organisms it was written for. Forcing it into the closest choice (the spider) gives a wrong name.
column29: Follow the centipede through step 1, then read both choices at step 2 carefully.

column9: An unknown organism is eukaryotic, multicellular and heterotrophic, has cell walls, and absorbs nutrients from a dead log. Which kingdoms can you rule out? Select all that apply.
column28: Eukaryotic rules out both bacteria kingdoms. Heterotrophic rules out Plantae, and having cell walls rules out Animalia. That leaves Fungi, which matches absorbing nutrients from a log, so it should not be ruled out.
column29: Use one clue at a time to cross off kingdoms.

column9: Which statements about the levels of classification are true? Select all that apply.
column14: Every member of order Carnivora is also in class Mammalia
column15: Every member of Kingdom Animalia is also in class Mammalia
column16: Every member of family Canidae is also in genus *Canis*
column17: Every member of class Mammalia is also in phylum Chordata
column18: Every member of genus *Canis* is also in family Canidae
column28: A smaller group always fits inside the larger group above it, so genus *Canis* is in Canidae, Mammalia is in Chordata, and Carnivora is in Mammalia. The reverse is not true: Canidae also includes foxes (*Vulpes*), and Animalia includes insects, fish and birds.
column29: Ask whether the first group is smaller than the second. A small group fits inside a big one, not the other way.

column9: Two animals are called pandas. The red panda is *Ailurus fulgens* (family Ailuridae). The giant panda is *Ailuropoda melanoleuca* (family Ursidae, the bear family). What does this show?
column14: A shared common name doesn't mean close relatives; these two are in different families
column16: The red panda is a kind of bear
column17: They are in the same genus because both genus names begin with Ailur-, and both are called pandas
column28: Their families differ, so they are in different genera and species too. The common name "panda" is misleading. *Ailurus* and *Ailuropoda* look alike, but they are different genus names, and similar spelling is the trap.
column29: Compare the family names, not the common names.

column9: The red maple is *Acer rubrum* and the red oak is *Quercus rubra*. Both species names mean "red." A student decides they must be in the same genus. Is she right?
column14: Yes; they are the same species
column15: No; the species word just describes a trait, and *Acer* and *Quercus* are different genera
column16: No; they are in different kingdoms
column17: Yes; when two species words have the same meaning, the two organisms must also share a genus
column28: The genus is the first word: *Acer* and *Quercus* are different genera. The second word describes a trait (red) and can repeat across very different organisms. Both trees are plants, so they are in the same kingdom.
column29: Which word of a scientific name tells you the genus?

column9: Linnaeus placed fungi in the plant kingdom. DNA evidence now shows fungi are more closely related to animals than to plants. Why might Linnaeus have grouped fungi with plants?
column15: Fungi and plants both stay in one place, and many grow from the ground, so they look alike
column16: Linnaeus compared the DNA of fungi and plants and found that their genes were nearly the same
column28: Linnaeus classified by visible structure, and fungi and plants both stay in one place and grow up from the soil. He had no DNA evidence. Fungi do not photosynthesize and do not have true leaves or roots.
column29: What could Linnaeus actually observe in the 1700s?

column9: Scientists find a microscopic organism in a Yellowstone hot spring. It is single-celled, has no nucleus, and its genetics are more complex than ordinary bacteria. Which domain and kingdom should it be placed in?
column28: No nucleus means prokaryote, so not Eukarya or Protista. An extreme home and complex genetics point to Archaebacteria, which is in Domain Archaea. Choosing Bacteria/Eubacteria uses only "no nucleus" and ignores the other clues.
column29: Use every clue: nucleus or not, then where it lives and its genetics.

column9: Put these groups that include humans in order from broadest to most specific.
column28: Kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata, class Mammalia, order Primates, family Hominidae, genus *Homo*. The common slip is swapping Primates and Hominidae; animal family names end in -idae, and families are below orders.
column29: Animal family names end in -idae, and *Homo* is the first word of *Homo sapiens*.

column9: The jaguar (*Panthera onca*) and the cougar (*Puma concolor*) both live in the Americas and are both large cats. The lion (*Panthera leo*) lives in Africa. Which is the jaguar's closest relative?
column28: The jaguar and lion share the genus *Panthera*, while the cougar is in a different genus, *Puma*. Living in the same place or looking alike is the trap; the shared genus shows the closer relationship.
column29: Ignore where they live. Compare the genus names.

column9: A student's key starts with "1a. Has fur → go to 2 / 1b. Has feathers → go to 3," but a frog is in the collection. What is the best fix?
column14: Make the two choices opposites, such as "Has fur" and "Does not have fur"
column15: Take the frog out of the collection
column16: Add the frog's name to choice 1a
column17: Add a third choice to step 1
column28: A good dichotomous step uses a trait and its opposite, so every organism fits exactly one choice. Adding a third choice breaks the two-choice rule, and removing the frog avoids the problem instead of fixing the key.
column29: Every organism should fit one choice or the other, with no third option.

column9: Organism A shares 5 levels (kingdom through family) with organism B, and 3 levels (kingdom through class) with organism C. How many levels do B and C share?
column28: B matches A down to family and C matches A down to class. So B and C both match A at kingdom, phylum and class, but C differs from A at order while B matches A there. B and C therefore differ at order: they share 3 levels. Answering 5 or 2 comes from adding or subtracting the numbers instead of comparing levels.
column29: Write out A's levels and mark how far down B and C each match.

column9: Organism Z is in the same order as organism Y but a different family. Organism X is in the same genus as organism Y. Which statement is true?
column14: X and Y are more closely related than Y and Z
column15: X and Z are in the same family
column16: Y and Z are more closely related than X and Y
column17: There is not enough information to compare them
column28: X and Y share a genus, which is more specific than the order that Y and Z share. X is in Y's family and Z is not, so X and Z cannot be in the same family.
column29: Which is more specific, genus or order?

column9: A student types the eastern chipmunk's name in a lab report in plain (not italic) letters as Striatus tamias. Its genus is *Tamias* and its species name is *striatus*. Which corrections are needed? Select all that apply.
column19: Add the family name in front
column28: The correct form is *Tamias striatus*: genus first and capitalized, species name second and lowercase, all in italics. The student got all four wrong. A family name is never part of a scientific name.
column29: Write the correct name yourself first, then compare it with the student's.

column9: Archaebacteria and Eubacteria are both prokaryotes, yet they are in different domains. Plants and fungi look very different, yet they share Domain Eukarya. What does this tell you about how domains are decided?
column14: Domains group organisms that look alike
column15: Domains are based on the size of the organism, so single-celled and many-celled living things are kept apart
column16: Domains are based on basic cell differences, like having a nucleus and how genetics work, not on looks
column17: Domains are based on where organisms live
column28: Domains are the broadest groups and are decided by cell structure and genetics. Plants and fungi both have a nucleus, so they share Eukarya. The two bacteria kingdoms differ in their genetics, so they are split. Grouping by looks is the mistake that the examples disprove.
column29: If looks decided domains, would plants and fungi be together?

column9: A water lily is multicellular, makes its own food by photosynthesis, has cellulose cell walls and lives in a pond. A student says it must be a protist because it lives in water. Which kingdom is correct?
column28: Its traits (multicellular, photosynthetic, cellulose cell walls) are the traits of Plantae. Habitat does not decide kingdom; many plants, animals and protists all live in water. Picking Protista because of the pond is the trap.
column29: Kingdoms are decided by cells and food, not by where an organism lives.

column9: Sea sponges stay attached to rocks as adults, and early naturalists thought they were plants. Today sponges are in Kingdom Animalia. Which evidence supports that?
column14: Sponges live in water, where many animals such as fish, crabs and sea stars also live
column16: Sponges do not move as adults
column17: Sponges are multicellular, have no cell walls and take in food rather than making it
column28: Being multicellular heterotrophs without cell walls matches Animalia. Living in water and color say nothing about kingdom, and not moving is the trait that fooled early naturalists into calling sponges plants.
column29: Which choice is about cells and how the sponge gets food?

column9: Students sort 30 organisms. All 30 are in Kingdom Animalia. 18 are in phylum Chordata, 10 of those are in class Mammalia, and 4 of those mammals are in order Carnivora. How many organisms are in Chordata but NOT in Mammalia?
column28: Mammalia fits inside Chordata, so the 10 mammals are part of the 18 chordates: 18 − 10 = 8. Subtracting the 4 carnivores as well (giving 4) is the common mistake; the carnivores are already inside the 10 mammals.
column29: Draw circles inside circles: Chordata holds Mammalia, which holds Carnivora.
